curriculum.lesson_evidence: Dancing in time means moving on the beat. Find the beat by listening for the steady pulse and tapping your foot. A rhythm pattern is a repeated group of long and short movements that fits over the beat. You can show a rhythm pattern with steps, claps and stamps: for example step, step, clap. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 to stay together. If you lose the beat, stop for a moment, listen and join in again on beat one. Keep stamping soft and wear safe shoes or bare feet.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Create a four-beat pattern using step, clap and rest. Write it as a list, and say which beat you would count the rest on.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Step, clap, step, rest. The rest happens on beat four, and I stay still but keep counting in my head.' A rest is a silent beat that still takes up time.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that if you are not moving, you are out of time. A rest is part of the rhythm, and counting inside your head helps you rejoin on the right beat.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Make a four-beat rhythm pattern and a different eight-beat pattern using at least three movements and one rest. Practise with a favourite song, counting aloud first. Teach one to someone at home and ask them to show if they stayed on the beat.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

Here is a more helpful example: Example: Max claps a steady beat and steps in a pattern of step, step, clap, rest over four beats. He says 1, 2, 3, 4 as he goes. The first step and second step each take one beat, the clap takes one beat and the rest is silent for one beat. When the music speeds up, his steps speed up evenly, so he is still in time.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally weak or disrespectful arts choice as a comparison. Name the specific error, then show a clearer or more respectful choice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same arts idea as the model, but with different content or material.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: Dancing in time means moving on the beat. Find the beat by listening for the steady pulse and tapping your foot. A rhythm pattern is a repeated group of long and short movements that fits over the beat. You can show a rhythm pattern with steps, claps and stamps: for example step, step, clap. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 to stay together. If you lose the beat, stop for a moment, listen and join in again on beat one. Keep stamping soft and wear safe shoes or bare feet. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.
